title: Disease burden of neonatal invasive Group B Streptococcus infection in the Netherlands (de Gier et al., PLoS One 2019;14(5):e0216749)

claims.text: Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae) is the leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis.
claims.byte_quote: Streptococcus agalactiae or group B Streptococcus (GBS) is the leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis.

claims.text: Early-onset GBS = invasive infection in the first 7 days of life; late-onset GBS = infection from one week up to three months of age (host age-band stratification).
claims.byte_quote: Invasive infections presenting within the first 7 days of life are categorized as 'early-onset GBS'. Infections presenting after one week, up to three months of age, are termed 'late-onset GBS'.

claims.text: Early-onset disease results from vertical transmission from the colonised mother; late-onset may also be nosocomial or community-transmitted (host exposure/risk factor).
claims.byte_quote: Early onset disease results from vertical transmission from the colonised mother, in late onset disease the pathogen may also be transmitted by nosocomial or community sources.

claims.text: GBS colonises the maternal intestinal and urogenital tract at a carriage rate of about 20% (host carriage risk factor for the neonate).
claims.byte_quote: GBS is part of the microbiome of the intestinal and urogenital tract, with a carriage rate of around 20%

claims.text: Estimated 97 cases and 6.5 deaths from culture-positive neonatal invasive GBS infection in the Netherlands in 2017 (population-specific incidence).
claims.byte_quote: An estimated 97 cases and 6.5 deaths occurred in the Netherlands in 2017 due to culture positive neonatal invasive GBS infection.
